messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Twelve years ago, Thang was coordinating supply routes for displaced families when an improvised explosive device detonated on the main road ahead. The blast shattered the windshield, threw him against the steering wheel, and filled the cabin with the acrid smell of cordite and burning rubber. Before he could pry himself free, the distant rumble of artillery and the panicked shouting of injured civilians bled into the heavy silence that followed. He remembered the exact shade of blue on the torn canvas of the aid truck and the sharp, metallic click of the driver’s jammed door. The event felt so violent and surreal that Thang now struggled to accept it had actually occurred; the details sat in his mind like a photograph he could not believe belonged to his own life. Those fractured images and the phantom echoes of shrapnel hitting metal surfaces would soon dictate his present reality. When a car backfired on the interstate near his community center, Thang’s body reacted before his mind could catch up. His chest tightened, his shoulders hunched forward, and he flinched violently at the ordinary noise. The sudden jolt of alertness kept him scanning the parking lot and the narrow aisles of the relief office, searching for threats that weren’t there. He stopped leaving the comfort of his kitchen and the quiet back room of the center, finding that only those specific, controlled spaces allowed his breathing to steady. That constant state of guard, however, only pulled the past deeper into his waking hours. Every time his hyperalert scanning caught an ordinary noise—a delivery truck idling too long outside his window, or a coffee mug clattering against a counter—the fear would snap shut like a trap, and the terrifying pictures would flood back. He would be staring at a routine grant proposal when the visual memory of the shattered dashboard overrode his focus, accompanied by the distinct, looping sound of the aid truck’s engine sputtering and dying. The threat monitoring itself acted as a key, unlocking the stored terror whenever his senses were caught off guard. To manage the relentless return of those scenes, Thang had built a quiet architecture of avoidance. He would sit for hours turning over the same questions in his head, repeatedly blaming himself for what happened, convinced that he had misjudged the route and that if he had only warned the driver to change lanes, everyone would have survived. The guilt hardened into a rigid rule: he would never enter a vehicle again, whether driving or riding as a passenger, because the confined space mirrored the trapped feeling of the wrecked cab. He applied the same logic to his daily environment at the refugee aid office. When funding cuts sparked tense debates among the staff, Thang withdrew immediately, refusing to voice a contrary opinion or step into any disagreement. He told himself it was to keep the peace, but the avoidance was really a way to keep the memory from spilling into the room. Over the months, the habits solidified into a quiet routine. He stopped accepting rides to the medical supply depot, taking long, circuitous walks that exhausted him and drew worried glances from his wife, Mei, who noticed how quickly his eyes darted to the door when the phone rang. At the center, he handled only backend inventory, stepping away before planning meetings reached any point of friction. The isolation crept into their marriage as well; he flinched when she placed a heavy set of keys on the counter, and he stopped suggesting restaurant outings because the noise of clinking silverware and overlapping conversations felt like a threshold he could no longer cross. Now, at seventy-two, Thang sits in a quiet office downtown, finally holding a referral slip from his primary care doctor. He has come to realize that the careful boundaries he built around himself are no longer keeping the past at bay but are instead shrinking his world to the size of a single room. What frightens him most is not the memories themselves, but the certainty that they will keep hijacking his nerves and that he is slowly losing the capacity to live in the present. He hopes, with a fragile kind of courage, that sitting in this chair might teach his mind a new way to breathe.
